title: On the rock
hook: the wise man built his house upon a rock (Matthew 7:24–27)
tomorrow: the result isn't up to you yet. what do you do while you wait?

segments.voice: Yesterday: my own beam, and Nathan's four words to a king. Today the Sermon on the Mount ends, in weather, and the crowd on the hill gets one last picture to take home.
screen: `MY OWN BEAM.` → `THE SERMON ENDS IN WEATHER.`

segments.voice: Rain on a roof, hard enough that people stop talking. Wind leaning on the windows. A gutter overflowing somewhere. That's the sound of the last story in the sermon, and yesterday's question has an answer: a house on rock in a storm sounds exactly as loud as the house next door. Two houses. One storm, the same for both. The difference isn't in the noise.
screen: `RAIN ON THE ROOF.` → `WIND ON THE WINDOWS.` → `TWO HOUSES, ONE STORM.`

segments.voice: Here's how Jesus ends. "Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock." Then the other builder, who hears the same sayings and doesn't do them, builds on sand. Same rain, same floods, same wind, "and great was the fall of it." Listen to what's the same. Both men heard. Same sermon, same words, same weather. The storm hits both houses. Doing the sayings, in this story, isn't a promise of no storms. The whole difference is one word: doeth. Not how much each man knew, not how well he understood, but whether he did it. And Matthew says when Jesus finished, "the people were astonished at his doctrine." That's the teaching Christians take from it: the sermon is meant to be lived, not admired. The letter of James says it plainly: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only." One to tell a friend: rock comes back later in Matthew, when Jesus says to Peter, "upon this rock I will build my church." The same picture, used twice.
screen: `HEARETH, AND DOETH.` · `THE STORM HITS BOTH HOUSES.` · `DOERS, NOT HEARERS ONLY.` · `UPON THIS ROCK.` · then, large: `ON THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Sit forward and press both feet flat into the floor until you feel the ground push back. Lay one hand on something solid, a table or a wall, and let a little of your weight rest there. Breathe as if the rain were outside and you were the house.
On the rock: the house of the one who hears the sayings and does them, still standing after the storm.
The line to keep: on the rock, which means doing, not only hearing. The Sermon on the Mount, read to the end.

howItsDone: Christians read the two builders (Matthew 7:24–27) as the Sermon on the Mount's closing call to live what it teaches; some children learn it as a song, and it is paired with James 1:22, be doers of the word.
